title: Pentagon Report Reveals 153 Civilians Killed in U.S. Yemen Strikes, Congress Demands Disclosure
excerpt: Internal Pentagon assessment finds three April 2025 airstrikes killed and wounded nearly 400 civilians during Operation Rough Rider, prompting congressional demands for full transparency.
body:
• Three U.S. airstrikes in Yemen in April 2025 killed 153 civilians and wounded 243, according to a Pentagon report submitted to Congress on Tuesday.
  • The report marks the first formal acknowledgment of civilian casualties during Operation Rough Rider, a 53-day bombing campaign against Iran-backed Houthi rebels.
  • Fifteen additional incidents remain under review; Congress has mandated full disclosure in the 2027 National Defense Authorization Act with funding leverage.
  • The conflict's impact on Red Sea shipping routes raises ongoing safety concerns for roughly 240,000 Indian seafarers and millions of Indian workers in the Gulf region.

The Pentagon has formally acknowledged that U.S. military operations killed 153 civilians and wounded 243 others in 2025, with all recorded casualties stemming from three airstrikes in Yemen during the Trump administration's campaign against Iran-backed Houthi rebels, according to a report submitted to Congress on Tuesday.

The figure represents a staggering increase from 2024, when the Pentagon assessed just two civilian deaths from U.S. military operations worldwide, and offers the first official accounting of the human toll from one of the most intensive American bombing campaigns in recent years.

The Toll of Operation Rough Rider

U.S. Central Command found that three strikes in April 2025 "more likely than not" resulted in civilian harm. The attacks were part of Operation Rough Rider, a 53-day campaign that targeted more than 1,000 Houthi positions across Yemen in an effort to stop the Iran-backed group from attacking commercial vessels in the Red Sea.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=mfc2PJburZU

The deadliest single attack struck the Ras Isa port in Hodeidah on April 17, 2025, hitting a major humanitarian aid hub with a large civilian workforce. The independent monitoring group Airwars documented 84 civilians killed and 150 wounded in that strike alone. A second attack on April 28 hit what Amnesty International identified as a migrant detention center, killing or wounding dozens of detainees whom Central Command had described only as occupants of "warehouse facilities."

President Trump declared a ceasefire in early May 2025 that ended the campaign, saying the Houthis would stop targeting ships. Officials and analysts said the strikes significantly degraded but did not eliminate the Houthi threat.

A Pattern of Delayed Disclosure

The report's release follows months of conflicting Pentagon communications. After Senator Elizabeth Warren pressed for casualty information, an assistant secretary acknowledged the three strikes warranted investigation. But weeks later, a senior defense official wrote to Warren claiming the Pentagon "has not assessed that civilian casualties have resulted from recent U.S. operations in Yemen since March 15, 2025" — a statement now directly contradicted by the department's own findings.

https://x.com/TheCradleMedia/status/2087456622062821749

"The Pentagon has gutted measures and mechanisms intended to prevent, mitigate and respond to civilian harm in U.S. military operations."

— Amanda Klasing, Amnesty International USA

A Department of Defense Inspector General investigation separately found that the Pentagon under Secretary Pete Hegseth has slashed funding and staff for civilian harm prevention programs, despite Congress mandating such protections in 2019 legislation.

Congressional Response

Lawmakers are pushing back with new legal tools. The 2027 National Defense Authorization Act requires the Pentagon to release unredacted civilian harm investigations for all three Yemen strikes, with provisions to withhold Defense Department funding — including travel money for Secretary Hegseth — if compliance lags.

The legislation also mandates disclosure of findings from a separate U.S. strike on a school in Minab, Iran, in February 2026 that killed more than 170 people, predominantly children. A Central Command investigation into that attack is nearly complete.

Impact on Indian Diaspora and Maritime Safety

The Yemen conflict's reverberations extend well beyond the immediate theater. India maintains approximately 240,000 active merchant seafarers — among the world's largest contingent — many of whom transit waters affected by Houthi operations. Just last week, an Indian-flagged cargo vessel, MSV Faize Noore Oliya, was attacked and sunk in the Red Sea off the Yemeni coast, with all 13 Indian crew members requiring rescue.

"The continuing incidents of attacks on commercial shipping in the region are deeply worrisome. Free and unimpeded navigation and commerce through international waterways must be restored at the earliest."

— India's Ministry of External Affairs

With an estimated 10 million Indian nationals living in the Gulf states and India's energy imports heavily dependent on Red Sea transit routes, the humanitarian and security dimensions of the Yemen conflict carry direct implications for the diaspora community.

What Comes Next

The Pentagon report does not account for casualties from more recent military operations, including strikes on vessels in the Caribbean and Eastern Pacific that have killed more than 200 people since September 2025. Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International have condemned those strikes as unlawful extrajudicial killings.

With 15 additional Yemen incidents still under review as of February 2026, the final civilian toll is likely to climb. The Pentagon has not responded to requests for comment on its initial denial of civilian casualties or its handling of congressional correspondence on the matter.
